young.html: Leo Tolstoy was a Russian count who lived on a big country estate. He wrote one of the longest and most famous novels in the world, War and Peace, about Russian families living through the years when the French emperor Napoleon tried to conquer Russia.

We follow a kind, clumsy young man named Pierre; a brave, proud prince named Andrew; and a lively, warm-hearted girl named Natasha, along with their families. There are parties, dances, hunts, friendships, mistakes and, in 1812, a terrible war, when Napoleon's huge army marches all the way to Moscow.

young.html: Tolstoy wondered: who really makes history? Is it emperors and generals, or millions of ordinary people each doing their part? He thought ordinary people matter much more than history books say.
For parents: the battle chapters describe the suffering of war plainly. Younger readers can enjoy the family chapters, such as Natasha's first ball and the wolf hunt, or a good abridgment.
History from below. Ask an older relative about an important event they lived through. What did they see, do or feel? Write it down. Tolstoy believed stories like theirs are the real history.

full.html: Count Leo Tolstoy (1828–1910) served as an artillery officer in the Crimean War, then settled at his estate, Yasnaya Polyana, where he ran a school for peasant children. He wrote War and Peace between 1863 and 1869, with his wife Sophia copying out the drafts by hand. It appeared in parts from 1865 to 1869. Louise and Aylmer Maude, friends of Tolstoy, translated it into English in 1922–23.

full.html: The novel follows several families, above all the warm, impractical Rostovs (Natasha, her brother Nicholas, young Petya, their cousin Sonya), the proud Bolkonskys (Prince Andrew, his devout sister Princess Mary, their stern old father), and Pierre Bezukhov, the awkward illegitimate son who suddenly inherits a fortune. It runs from 1805, when Russia fights Napoleon in Austria, to 1812, when Napoleon invades Russia, and ends in 1820.
At the Battle of Austerlitz in 1805, Prince Andrew, dreaming of glory, falls wounded with a flag in his hands:

full.text: Above him there was now nothing but the sky—the lofty sky, not clear yet still immeasurably lofty, with gray clouds gliding slowly across it. ... How was it I did not see that lofty sky before? And how happy I am to have found it at last!

full.html: When Napoleon invades, the families scatter. At Borodino, Pierre wanders the battlefield and Andrew is wounded again; Moscow is abandoned and burns; Pierre, taken prisoner, meets the peasant soldier Platon Karataev, whose simple goodness changes him. In the long retreat the French army is destroyed by cold, hunger and pursuit. In the end Pierre marries Natasha, and Nicholas marries Princess Mary.

full.text:
A king is history's slave.

History, that is, the unconscious, general, hive life of mankind, uses every moment of the life of kings as a tool for its own purposes.
full.author: Tolstoy
full.work: War and Peace, Book Nine, Chapter I

full.html: Tolstoy interrupts his story with essays arguing that Napoleon's genius was an illusion: battles and wars are decided by the countless choices of ordinary people, and great men only seem to lead. The old general Kutuzov, who waits and lets events unfold, is wiser than Napoleon, who thinks he commands them. The second Epilogue is a long essay on free will and necessity.

Readers argue about these essays. Many critics, and some historians, find Tolstoy's view too sweeping: leaders' decisions do sometimes change events. Others think he was right to turn attention to ordinary people. The philosopher Isaiah Berlin, in a famous 1953 essay, called Tolstoy a "fox" who saw many things but longed to be a "hedgehog" who knows one big thing.
Expecting a single hero. War and Peace has many centers; its real subject is life itself, in families, friendships and nations, and how people find meaning in it.

deep.text: War and Peace in the great conversation

items: Homer's Iliad: Tolstoy saw himself writing a modern epic, with war seen from every side.
Hegel, earlier in this era, made "world-historical individuals" like Napoleon the agents of history; Tolstoy answers him directly.
Thucydides and Gibbon, earlier on this ladder, explain wars by leaders' decisions and causes; Tolstoy doubts such explanations.
Dostoevsky, the next Russian on this ladder, asked about faith and freedom in a darker key.
Do great leaders make history, or does history make them?
Where do people find meaning: in glory, in learning, in family, in faith?
Why might the most important changes in a life come in quiet moments, like Andrew's sky?
Can a person be both free and part of something much larger?

questions: Which character would you most like to be friends with? Why?
Prince Andrew wanted glory, then found peace looking at the sky. Have you ever changed your mind about what matters?
Natasha gave the family's carts to wounded soldiers. What does that tell you about her?
Tolstoy said ordinary people make history. What ordinary person do you admire?
Why do you think Tolstoy called the book War and Peace?
